column3: The immediate continuation makes restraint necessary when marriage is unavailable until God grants sufficiency from His favor.
Its servant-status and divine judgment offer only a remote channel-level resonance with household provision.
The false claim that God is poor reverses the focus ayah's dependence: people need God, not the reverse.
Poverty is set against God's promise of forgiveness and favor, directly supporting confidence beyond fear of lack.
The surah's enacted legal frame supplies broad context but adds no specific account of marriage or provision.
Moses explicitly names his need for whatever good God sends, giving a personal instance of dependence and provision.
It explicitly contrasts human poverty with God's self-sufficiency and ties that dependence to communal spending.
Universal divine ownership is a general ground for provision but is less specific than the poverty parallels.
It directly names people as needy before God and God as self-sufficient, grounding the focus ayah's promise of enrichment.
A pledge to give charity when granted divine favor shows favor as provision with a social obligation.
The nearby sexual-law setting gives only broad context for the surah's ordered marital life.
Its marriage prohibition shows that forming households is regulated by durable kinship boundaries, not mere availability.
God's favor is given as He wills and the verse closes with the same vast-knowing attributes, though outside marriage and poverty.
It treats marriage as a socially accountable bond, complementing the focus ayah's command to arrange such bonds.
Wealth and earnings failing to suffice provide a limited contrast to sufficiency granted by God.
The identical vast-knowing formula is an attribute echo without a marriage or poverty setting.
After marital separation, God can make each party sufficient from His abundance, a direct marital sufficiency parallel.
It identifies concealed poverty and directs giving toward it, clarifying the communal responsibility around need.
Material breadth is denied as the sole measure of fitness, while God grants authority; this is only an indirect capacity parallel.
The local protection of sexual reputation supports the surah's social order but not the provision promise itself.
Marriage to righteous men cannot provide security before God, limiting what a marital bond itself can supply.
Marriage readiness, wealth stewardship, and different treatment of rich and poor guardians connect household capacity to accountable care.
God's ownership and freedom from need give a broad theological basis for provision without making it dependent on human exchange.
It commands arranging marriages across free and enslaved status while prioritizing faith, closely paralleling the focus ayah's social mandate.
Fear of economic loss is answered by God's promise to enrich from His favor, directly echoing the focus ayah's assurance.
Repentance restores standing within the local legal sequence but adds no distinct marriage-and-provision relation.
It tersely presents poverty followed by divine enrichment, the central movement of the focus ayah.
The same vast-knowing formula and freely given favor are a repeated attribute-level parallel.
The spouse-specific testimony procedure adds legal context but no distinct insight into marriage or poverty.
The anticipated calamity does not materially clarify marital provision or divine enrichment.
The righteous named here loosely echo the focus ayah's righteous household members, without its marital or economic claim.
Retaliation and patience do not add to the focus ayah's household-sufficiency reading.
Wealth and children cannot avail against God, contrasting human assets with the divine sufficiency promised in the focus.
God's added favor to believers is a general provision echo without the poverty or marriage dimension.
The oath formula in the local procedure adds no new connection.
Food that does not relieve hunger supplies a narrow contrast to genuine sufficiency.
It forbids obstructing remarriage when the parties agree properly, reinforcing communal responsibility to permit lawful households.
The contrast between an incapable owned servant and one given provision who spends it relates status, provision, and circulation of resources.
Being preoccupied on the final day is not the material self-sufficiency at issue.
Communal religious maintenance is only a distant institutional setting for the social order of the focus ayah.
The reciprocal oath procedure adds no distinct relation to household capacity.
God's self-sufficiency despite universal disbelief clarifies that divine giving is not compelled by human return.
Household access and the ban on later marriage to the Prophet's wives show marriage as a protected social institution.
Unequal provision and withholding it from owned dependents expose a material contrast to the focus ayah's inclusive household concern.
A shelter that cannot protect from flame is a distant negative image of failed sufficiency.
Reward from divine favor is a general grace echo already covered by stronger provision parallels.
The concluding oath formula adds no distinct relation.
Stinginess joined to claimed self-sufficiency directly contrasts with the focus ayah's reliance on God-given provision.
Those with means who seek exemption offer a limited contrast between possessing wealth and using it responsibly.
Chastity and miraculous birth touch the sexual-protection context only indirectly.
Giving charity to the poor makes the communal material response to need explicit.
The Prophet's distress over disbelief does not clarify marriage or poverty.
Divine favor and mercy in the same surah form a general local echo without the focus ayah's provision claim.
God owns all and is self-sufficient, supporting the asymmetry behind His ability to enrich households.
Security after fear is a broad social blessing but not a specific marital or poverty parallel.
Marital repair must reckon with possessiveness, adding a relational pressure that household arrangements must address.
The self-sufficient and merciful Lord can replace people, reinforcing that divine mercy is not born of need.
Disassociation and reliance here do not materially develop the focus ayah's household provision.
The false-report episode has no specific connection to marriage capacity or poverty.
God's independence after rejection confirms that human refusal cannot diminish the source of sufficiency.
Even doubled earthly wealth cannot ransom judgment, a distant limit on material self-reliance.
Narrative timing at sunrise offers no relevant household or provision reading.
Its limits on remarriage after divorce show that marital reunion is ordered by conditions rather than simple private choice.
The fragment about worship objects adds no material connection.
The demand for a good assumption in the false-report episode does not clarify the focus ayah.
Temporary worldly enjoyment failing to avail gives a general contrast to lasting sufficiency.
The rejection of others' worship adds no relevant provision or marriage relation.
Servitude to God limits claims of self-sufficiency, but the connection is remote from the household mandate.
Human alliances cannot avail before God, offering only a broad contrast to divine sufficiency.
Prospective reconciliation with former enemies does not clarify marital provision.
The departure command supplies no material connection.
Claimed self-sufficiency is named as the condition of transgression, contrasting with the focus ayah's dependence on God.
When full marital means are lacking, it provides a regulated route to marriage with believing enslaved women and due payment.
Poverty caused by displacement and loss of home and property gives a concrete social form of need seeking God's favor.
Human schemes and outside help failing to avail give a distant contrast to genuine divine sufficiency.
Lawful spoils and piety do not materially clarify the household provision claim.
Specified alms recipients make organized support for poverty and vulnerability explicit, though not marriage-specific.
A person's wealth failing at ruin repeats the limit of material self-sufficiency.
Kinship affection and increased good works do not add to the focus ayah's central relation.
Provision and a gracious release after an unconsummated marriage show material responsibility at the end of a household bond.
The self-sufficient person's social prominence repeats the contrary posture already established by 96:7.
Thanksgiving after deliverance does not add a household or poverty connection.
It warns against leaving a wife suspended and directs repair, adding a distinct concern for marital justice.
Conjecture cannot suffice for truth, but this is a nonmaterial use of the same sufficiency language.
Careful reform of orphans supports responsible household integration, though it is not a marriage or enrichment passage.
The denial of rival protectors and account of enjoyment do not clarify the focus reading.
Accumulated numbers and pride fail to suffice, a general contrast to reliance on divine favor.
The inability to find means before required charity gives a limited glimpse of material constraint.
Kind speech and forgiveness are better than harmful charity, qualifying how support for need should be given.
Objection to God distributing His favor shows favor is granted by divine choice, but lacks the focus's household setting.
The promise of gardens to believers does not materially clarify marriage or poverty.
The command to fear God and obey adds no distinct relation.
Provision within communal rites gives a broad religious setting, without a direct household-capacity link.
It assigns provision and clothing within a nursing household according to capacity, a concrete family-support parallel.
Divine sustaining ownership and encompassing knowledge broadly support the closing vast-knowing attributes.
The catalog of favors to Jesus does not add a material marriage or poverty relation.
A gift is recognized as the Lord's favor while God remains rich, a general grace-and-independence echo.
Obedient fear of the Lord does not clarify the focus ayah's household provision.
Praise and prostration add no relevant marital or economic connection.
Being turned away from the message does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Righteousness includes giving cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy, making communal provision a central obligation.
It identifies close kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers as recipients of spending, directly supplying the focus ayah's social support horizon.
The command to give what exceeds need frames material capacity as something that can circulate to others.
Reciprocal rights within divorce and waiting periods add a household-accountability frame to the focus ayah's marriage mandate.
Retention in kindness or release in kindness establishes ethical limits for ending the households the focus ayah seeks to form.
It protects the waiting period before a new marriage, showing that household formation is temporally and publicly ordered.
Even an unconsummated divorce requires provision according to means, directly joining marriage to material responsibility.
The required half-gift after divorce makes the marital bond carry a concrete material claim.
Provision and residence for widows extend household responsibility beyond the husband's death.
Giving respite or remitting a debt addresses economic hardship, though outside the marital setting.
Marriage to women in the care of guardians is conditioned by justice, linking household formation to protection of vulnerability.
The command to give women their bridal gifts makes material provision an integral element of marriage.
It requires honorable treatment of wives and rejects coercive retention of their property, qualifying the household established by marriage.
Marriage is joined to specified bridal gifts and honorable conduct, directly connecting lawful union with material obligation.
It directs people to seek God's favor rather than covet unequal shares, a relevant account of provision and dependence.
It explicitly grounds household maintenance in what men spend from their wealth, supplying a central economic dimension of marriage.
Family-appointed reconciliation addresses the repair of marital breakdown within the social order envisioned by the focus ayah.
It requires justice for vulnerable female orphans whom guardians wish to marry, directly joining marriage, dependency, and communal duty.
Feeding or clothing needy people as expiation is a secondary but concrete practice of meeting material lack.
It commands giving the due share at harvest, placing provision within an obligation of distribution.
It assigns a due share to kin, the needy, and travelers, directly supporting a community that addresses lack.
It rejects both miserly withholding and ruinous spending, qualifying the responsible use of resources in household life.
God expands and restricts provision as He wills, framing material capacity as divinely administered rather than self-produced.
It rejects killing children from fear of poverty because God provides for both parents and children, directly countering economic fear around family formation.
Guarding sexual parts supplies the chastity discipline that precedes and bounds the lawful unions of the focus ayah.
Its exception for spouses and owned dependents situates sexual access within defined household relations.
The pairing of good women with good men gives a nearby account of marital suitability and reciprocal household formation.
The command to lower the gaze and guard chastity supplies the preparatory restraint surrounding lawful marriage.
Women's chastity and regulated disclosure likewise locate marriage within protected social boundaries.
Balanced spending between extravagance and miserliness gives a practical norm for sustaining a household.
Spouses are described as a source of dwelling, affection, and mercy, directly defining the human good that marriage is meant to establish.
Its detailed permissions and bridal gifts confirm that marriage relations are legally structured and materially marked.
God's widening and restricting of provision reinforces that wealth is not a stable measure of worth or capacity.
Whatever is spent is promised recompense from God, directly supporting communal generosity in response to need.
Private and public spending from divine provision links received sustenance to its circulation.
God's expansion and restriction of provision provide a broad theological context for the focus ayah's promise of enrichment.
The keys of the heavens and earth and differentiated provision reinforce divine control of household capacity.
Unlimited provision could lead to excess, adding a restraint-oriented qualification to the promise of sufficiency.
The distribution of livelihoods and social ranks frames provision as allotted by God rather than owned as independent status.
The creation of pairs offers a broad structural resonance with the focus ayah's command to marry the unpaired.
The creation of male and female is a distant basis for the paired human relation at issue.
It regulates the dissolution and continuation of marriages across migration and faith, including the return of marital payments.
Compensation for lost marital payments makes material justice part of the regulation of broken marriages.
Divorce is followed by a promise of an opening for those who remain mindful of God, offering a transition parallel to marital need.
God provides from an unforeseen source and suffices the one who relies on Him, directly illuminating the focus ayah's promise beyond present poverty.
It requires housing and support for divorced pregnant wives, making family provision concrete even after separation.
Support is explicitly measured by means, while the constrained person gives from what God has given, directly addressing household capacity under poverty.
A known share of wealth is reserved for the needy, making provision a regular social practice.
It specifies both the asking and deprived needy as recipients, sharpening attention to visible and hidden lack.
Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite personal desire for the food exemplifies provision that exceeds self-interest.
Human creation in pairs is only a broad anthropological parallel to arranging marriage.
Failure to honor the orphan marks the social neglect that the focus ayah's community-oriented mandate resists.
Failure to urge feeding the poor gives a negative counterpart to communal action on material need.
Feeding in a day of severe hunger directly depicts a decisive response to acute poverty.
Care for a related orphan identifies a vulnerable household member as a priority of provision.
Feeding a destitute person in dust gives a vivid endpoint of poverty requiring aid.
Giving wealth while remaining mindful of God offers the positive counterpart to miserly self-sufficiency.
Spending wealth for purification reinforces generosity as a practice not governed by self-enrichment.
Failure to encourage feeding the poor is treated as a grave social failure, directly contrasting with organized response to need.
Kindness to parents, kin, orphans, and the needy gives an earlier communal ethic of care for vulnerable dependents.
Relatives, orphans, and the needy present at inheritance are to receive provision, extending household wealth beyond its direct heirs.
Its command to do good to kin, orphans, and the needy supplies a broad social-care framework for vulnerable households.
Faith and spending from God's provision unite trust in God with material generosity.
Private consultation is commended when it promotes charity, goodness, or reconciliation, a secondary institutional support for need and households.
Protection of orphan property until maturity safeguards the material base from which vulnerable persons can enter adult households.
God makes spouses and descendants and provides good things, directly joining family formation with divine provision.
Those with means are commanded to give to relatives, the needy, and emigrants, providing a nearby surah model of support from surplus.
The prayer for spouses and descendants as comfort gives the household sought by the focus ayah an explicit moral horizon.
God provides for creatures unable to carry their own provision, reinforcing reliance beyond visible means.
God's expansion and restriction of provision support the focus ayah's confidence that present poverty is not final capacity.
A community is directed to eat from its Lord's provision and give thanks, placing collective prosperity under divine gift.
Wealth and children do not themselves bring nearness to God, limiting their use as a measure of household success.
People are stewards over what has been placed in their hands and are commanded to spend from it, strengthening the focus ayah's communal obligation.
Giving to God is described as a loan multiplied in return, encouraging the circulation of resources to meet need.
The hosts prefer impoverished migrants over themselves despite need, a particularly clear communal response to poverty.
Spending for one's own good is joined to mindfulness and resistance to possessiveness, directly countering withholding.
Failure to feed the poor is among the defining admissions of wrongdoing, sharply underscoring social responsibility for need.
Guardians must feed and clothe those not yet able to manage property, giving a direct model of household provision for dependents.
It forbids killing children from poverty and grounds the prohibition in God's provision for parents and children.
Every creature's provision rests with God, giving a broad but direct ground for trust beyond present resources.
God expands and restricts provision, reinforcing that material breadth is divinely apportioned rather than a fixed personal status.
Believers are urged to spend from what they have been provided before exchange and friendship fail, strengthening the urgency of circulation.
The promise of a good life for faithful action offers a broad ethical horizon but not a specific household-provision claim.
Provision in the Garden offers an eschatological echo of divinely supplied sufficiency.
God commands prayer while denying that He seeks provision from people; He is the one who provides, directly clarifying divine independence.
Divinely provided livestock are to be remembered over and used in a shared ritual economy, linking provision with communal practice.
Sacrificial food is to be shared with the content and the needy, making received provision socially distributive.
The question of who begins creation and provides from heaven and earth supplies a broad theological ground for the promise of enrichment.
It directs people to seek provision from God and worship Him, explicitly locating sustenance with the divine source.
Those given provision spend from it, joining dependence on God to an active response toward others.
The earth and sky are presented as a habitable setting furnished with good provisions, a distant creation-and-sustenance parallel.
God declares no need for provision from people, sharply establishing the divine independence underlying His giving.
God is explicitly the Provider and possessor of enduring strength, a direct theological companion to the focus ayah's enrichment promise.
Seeking God's bounty after communal worship gives a broad, nonmarital provision echo.
People are directed to move through the earth and eat from God's provision, locating livelihood in a received gift.
The promise of wealth and children gives a limited prosperity parallel without the focus ayah's household mandate.
The command to give a good loan to God reinforces voluntary material support as a faithful use of provision.
